title: Facts, stats and trivia ahead of the 2026 United States GP
excerpt:
The 2026 Formula 1 season continues this weekend as Austin hosts Round 18 on the calendar, the United States Grand Prix.

Free Practice 1 and 2 will take place on Friday, October 23, followed by Free Practice 3 and Qualifying on Saturday, October 24, and the Grand Prix itself on Sunday, October 25.

Vital statistics

First Grand Prix – 1959 (Sebring)

Track Length – 5.513km

Lap record – 1m 36.169s, Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, 2019

Most pole positions – Michael Schumacher and Lewis Hamilton (4)

Most wins – Lewis Hamilton (6)

Trivia – In 2022, Austin set a then F1 record with a three-day attendance of around 440,000 fans

Pole run to Turn 1 braking point – 230 metres

Overtakes completed in 2025 – 71

Safety Car probability – 29%*

Virtual Safety Car probability – 43%*

Pit stop time loss – 19.90 seconds

*From the last seven races in Austin

The driver’s verdict

Jolyon Palmer, former Renault F1 driver: The Circuit of The Americas is a great track that takes inspiration from parts of other legendary corners on the calendar.

The uphill Turn 1 is difficult at the race start as there are loads of different lines that can be taken, then you sweep through the first sector, which is a bit like Silverstone, where you’re trying to find your rhythm.

After that, it’s the long back straight and you’ve got to get your braking point right at the end of it…

Probably the hardest section on the circuit is Turn 13 through to Turn 15, which feels like an odd complex of corners behind the wheel. Turn 13 is conventional, but finding your line through to 15 is not easy, while that Turn 14 area puts a lot of load on the tyres.

You go through the quadruple right-hander after that, followed by Turn 19, which is a really nice corner – though track limits are an issue.

Finally, you stop for Turn 20, then it’s a short burst to the line, but drivers need to be careful not to light things up as it’s easy to break traction.

Everything you need to know about the Circuit of The Americas

Last five United States GP polesitters

2025 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2024 – Lando Norris (McLaren)

2023 – Charles Leclerc (Ferrari)

2022 – Carlos Sainz (Ferrari)

2021 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

Last five United States GP winners

2025 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2024 – Charles Leclerc (Ferrari)

2023 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2022 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2021 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

Tyre and strategy insight

“The Austin circuit, which is 5.513 kilometres long, features a mix of high-speed corners, rapid direction changes and slower sections that demand strong traction,” reads Pirelli’s weekend preview, with the tyre selection for the event seeing the C2 used as the hard, the C3 as the medium and the C4 as the soft.

“To be competitive, teams must combine good straight-line speed with efficient aerodynamic load through the more technical sections, an aspect that becomes even more important with the current generation of Formula 1 cars.

“From a tyre perspective, COTA places demands on both axles. In the first sector, characterised by fast corners and direction changes inspired by some of Europe’s great circuits, the front tyres will be placed under particular stress. In the third sector, meanwhile, the numerous acceleration zones out of slow corners will tend to generate thermal degradation primarily on the rear tyres.

“The asphalt surface is not particularly abrasive. A section of the circuit between Turns 9 and 11 was resurfaced earlier this year. However, the ageing effect on the remainder of the track continues to be significant and contributes to high wear levels. Tyre wear, rather than graining, could therefore prove to be one of the key factors over the weekend. During last year's event, several tyres reached very high wear values.

“Track grip is generally good, aided by the support categories, including the Porsche Carrera Cup North America, which has been supplied by Pirelli since the start of this year. Track evolution, on the other hand, has traditionally not been among the most pronounced on the calendar.

“From a strategic standpoint, the presence of the C2 as the hard compound could favour long stints, offering teams a solid option for what is likely to be a one-stop race. However, the high temperatures that typically characterise the Texan weekend must also be taken into account, as they could increase degradation and open the door to alternative strategies.”

Current form

As has been the case since Round 3 in Japan, Kimi Antonelli remains at the top of the drivers’ standings – but this weekend marks the first in which the Italian has a mathematical chance of sealing his maiden title.

For this to happen, Antonelli would need to win the race with Mercedes team mate George Russell finishing ninth or lower and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton placing no higher than fifth. Can the 20-year-old become the youngest-ever World Champion in Austin?

While Antonelli and the Silver Arrows continue to head the standings, it is Max Verstappen and Red Bull who have been leading the way on track at the last two rounds, the Dutchman scoring back-to-back victories in Malaysia and Singapore.

Verstappen holds a strong record at the Circuit of The Americas, having triumphed in four of F1’s last five visits to the track – and the four-time World Champion will doubtless be keen to add to that run.

Elsewhere, McLaren will be hoping for a stronger weekend after Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri’s clash in the Singapore Sprint, while Ferrari also experienced mixed fortunes in Marina Bay, with Charles Leclerc securing a podium result as Hamilton slipped backwards following a backfired strategy.

Behind them, Racing Bulls have further strengthened their hold on P5 in the midfield battle – now holding an advantage of 32 points over sixth-placed Alpine – while Haas arrive into the event days after confirming that rookie Rafael Camara will join the team in 2027.

Iconic moment

The inaugural Austin race back in 2012 was an exhilarating watch, with Lewis Hamilton chasing down Red Bull’s Sebastian Vettel in his McLaren.

After Vettel lost momentum behind a backmarker, Hamilton sensed his opportunity to pounce for the lead – and the Briton duly took his chance.

title: Everything you need to know about the Circuit of The Americas
excerpt:
The 2026 Formula 1 season heads to Texas this weekend for the United States Grand Prix, as Austin’s Circuit of The Americas prepares to welcome the drivers for Round 18 of the campaign. But how much do you know about the famous American venue? F1.com has your all-in-one guide…

Key Circuit of The Americas statistics

Circuit length: 5.513km

Number of turns: 20

Number of laps: 56

Race distance: 308.405km

Lap record: 1m 36.169s – Charles Leclerc (2019)

When was Austin’s first Grand Prix?

The Circuit of The Americas made its Formula 1 debut in 2012, becoming the first purpose-built F1 venue in the United States and marking the championship’s return to the country after a five-year absence.

It was designed by renowned circuit architect Hermann Tilke and the track takes inspiration from some of F1’s most famous corners, including Silverstone’s Maggots and Becketts sequence and the sweeping turns in the stadium section of Hockenheim in Germany.

The inaugural race was won by Lewis Hamilton, who overtook Sebastian Vettel to claim his final victory for McLaren before his switch to Mercedes. The Briton has since become the most successful F1 driver in COTA’s history, with five victories to his name.

What’s the circuit like to drive?

The 5.513km circuit combines high-speed changes of direction with tight, technical corners. Meanwhile, the steep uphill approach to Turn 1 and blind apex offers one of the most dramatic starts to a lap anywhere on the calendar.

With 20 corners and several overtaking opportunities, drivers need to balance speed and precision throughout the lap, particularly through the opening sector and the more technical final sector.

Jolyon Palmer, former Renault F1 driver, explained: “The Circuit of The Americas is a great track that takes inspiration from parts of other legendary corners on the calendar.

“The uphill Turn 1 is difficult at the race start as there are loads of different lines that can be taken, then you sweep through the first sector, which is a bit like Silverstone, where you’re trying to find your rhythm.

“After that, it’s the long back straight and you’ve got to get your braking point right at the end of it.

“Probably the hardest section on the circuit is Turn 13 through to Turn 15, which feels like an odd complex of corners behind the wheel. Turn 13 is conventional, but finding your line through to 15 is not easy, while that Turn 14 area puts a lot of load on the tyres.

“You go through the quadruple right-hander after that, followed by Turn 19, which is a really nice corner – though track limits are an issue.

“Finally, you stop for Turn 20, then it’s a short burst to the line, but drivers need to be careful not to light things up as it’s easy to break traction."

"The Circuit of The Americas is a great track that takes inspiration from parts of other legendary corners on the calendar."Jolyon Palmer

Where are the Straight Mode zones and overtake detection?

As a reminder, and as explained in our pre-season summary of regulation changes, Straight Mode is a different aerodynamic configuration that allows cars to reduce their drag, making them more efficient when accelerating up towards top speed.

The rear wing continues to open up a gap – just like it did when drivers used DRS (the Drag Reduction System) in the past – but now the front wing also moves. The uppermost front wing elements drop down at the same time the rear wing’s top element does.

This is a mode that is used on every single lap in dry conditions, in every area that is designated for it. Essentially, the car will adapt between two different configurations depending on where it is on the track, providing maximum downforce in corners but then less drag on straights.

In Austin, there are two designated Straight Mode zones – the first is located between Turns 11 and 12, while the second runs along the start/finish straight after Turn 20 into Turn 1.

Meanwhile, Overtake Mode replaces DRS and is a new power mode that allows a driver to recharge more electrical energy, and generate an additional electrical power profile, so they can sustain a higher speed for a longer period.

There is one detection point per lap for this mode – expected to be out of the final corner on many occasions, leading onto a long straight – and it will be available to drivers on the following lap as long as they stay within a second of the car in front at that detection point.

Around the Circuit of The Americas, the Overtake Detection point comes as drivers head out of Turn 20, while the Overtake Activation line follows on the start/finish straight.

Five fun facts about the United States Grand Prix

Everything really is bigger in Texas! For 2026, COTA is unveiling what is set to be the world’s largest cowboy hat, measuring 75 feet long, with a themed bar underneath. The attraction will be located in the circuit’s Lone Star Land fan area.

Lewis Hamilton has clinched two of his seven World Drivers’ Championships at COTA, securing his third title in 2015 and his sixth in 2019.

Before Austin took over in 2012, five other circuits hosted the United States Grand Prix – Sebring, Riverside, Watkins Glen, Phoenix and Indianapolis.

F1 ACADEMY will return to COTA this year for the first time since its inaugural season in 2023, with the series set to stage three races across the weekend.

Mercedes hold the record for the most wins in COTA with five victories to date, while Red Bull are close behind with four.

title: How F1 drivers and strategists tackle the Circuit of The Americas
excerpt:
The US Grand Prix at the Circuit of The Americas is one of the great tent-pole events of the Formula 1 calendar. It is simply immense, drawing in vast crowds, celebrity guests and a stupendous TV audience. It’s a superb circuit that has always produced interesting races, and right from year one has been a firm favourite with the teams.

COTA is a good place to race – but that’s not the same as being an easy place to race. The track makes harsh demands on an F1 car. It’s very fast, but also very bumpy; the first sector demands a car that works well in high-speed, but elsewhere the lap wants one that excels in low-speed – and you really can’t set-up for both.

And while engineers are dealing with that conundrum, drivers need to figure out how to approach a Qualifying lap: push too hard at the start and the tyres give up before the end. The 'Goldilocks Zone’ is as ephemeral as the morning mist in Travis County.

So how will the teams, drivers and strategists approach the weekend? It’s time to take a look in The Risk Perspective, in partnership with Marsh, Formula 1's Official Risk Partner and Official Insurance Brokering Partner.

The Engineering Perspective: Xavi Marcos Padros

Xavi Marcos Padros has vast experience on both sides of the Atlantic, having worked in F1 for HRT, Williams and Ferrari, around a spell as chief race engineer for Richard Childress Racing in NASCAR. He joined Cadillac in 2025, working on its WEC and IMSA programmes, before becoming chief race engineer for the Cadillac F1 Team.

“The different sectors at COTA pose some really good questions for set-up, with no obviously right or wrong answers. A lot depends on your car: you might get the best results optimizing around the high-speed corners at the start of the lap, or around the lower speed sections at the end.

“The surface is quite rough – but that doesn’t really change our set-up discussions because we’re asking the same questions about how best to maximise what we have, no matter the limitations of any particular circuit.

“We’ll discuss damper settings, general stiffnesses to cope with any bumps, try to maximise ride-height for those, and also, of course, to make sure we are legal at the end of the race with the amount of wear to the plank [the composite board attached to the bottom of the car, which is measured post-race to ensure a minimum ride height].

“Our initial set-up for FP1 is based on simulator and simulation data, and then we’ll make adjustments for FP2, based on what we saw in FP1. We’ll have some simulator sessions overnight on Friday to optimize the setup for Saturday, but we’ll also take into account the drivers’ feedback. Some can cope with a stiffer set-up, others need something a little softer. We’ll factor all of these things into our decisions.

5 storylines we're excited about ahead of the US Grand Prix

“Getting a Qualifying lap right is very difficult, because there are risks involved. It is a tough lap for the tyres: if the out-lap prepares them well so they are ready for the first sector then they overheat in the final sector, which is very tough on the left side of the car through the long right-hand corners.

“We can compromise, and perhaps do the first sector with tyres that aren’t quite up to temperature, so they are better in the final part of the lap – but it can be difficult to know which is the best approach. We’ll practice this on Friday, trying different sorts of out-lap, and than plan a cross-car test for our final Qualifying sims in FP3… but it can be a moving target because rubber will go down, grip will increase and the track will evolve."

The Strategy

In strategy terms, COTA has tended to be one of the more interesting circuits on the F1 calendar, being on the cusp between one and two stops. Between 2021-23 it was a two-stop race, being won by medium>hard>hard in ’21, medium>hard>medium in ’22, and medium>medium>hard in ’23.

For 2024 it dropped to a medium>hard one-stop and, last year, Pirelli tried something different with a compound bridge: instead of the usual C2-C3-C4, they bought C1-C3-C4, with the hope of a tortoise-and-hare scenario, of steady one-stoppers using the hard compound battling in the final laps with the more rapid two-stoppers running the softer compounds.

It didn’t work out that way, with the race being entirely a one-stop affair… on the softer tyres, Max Verstappen won with a medium>soft race. This year, Pirelli go back to the conventional C2-C3-C4.

The race we get at COTA often depends on the temperatures, with Texas at the end of October capable of going either way. At the time of writing, the forecast is for hot weather, which tends to increase degradation, but two-stop races have been a rarity in 2026…

The Drivers’ Perspective: Colton Herta

Colton Herta is Cadillac’s test and reserve driver, and will be taking part in FP1 this weekend, substituting for Sergio Perez for one of the team’s mandatory rookie sessions. This is his fourth FP1 session of the season, having already appeared in Barcelona, Budapest and at Monza.

Despite being only 26, he has vast experience as a racing driver, having completed seven series in IndyCar, winning nine times and finishing second in the 2024 Championship. The first of his nine victories came here at COTA, back in 2019 – when he became the youngest driver to ever win in IndyCar.

“The right set-up is always a difficult question to answer for this track because the different sections ask quite different things of the car. One of the biggest challenges is how bumpy it is and finding the right balance between ride heights and overall stiffness. You’re trying to get something that works well through the high-speed first sector but still gives you what you need in the longer, slower corners.

“Wind can also change which parts of the track you can maximize, so that adds another factor to think about. With the unusual mix of corners, you’re never going to feel completely comfortable or happy everywhere. It’s about finding a happy medium across the whole lap.

“The biggest thing you have to remind yourself is that you’re never going to feel completely comfortable on a lap here. That’s just part of the challenge of driving at COTA, and you have to keep that in mind when you’re judging how the car feels.

“From a set-up point of view, you’re trying to find the best compromise between dealing with the bumps and getting the balance you want around the rest of the lap. You can work towards something that feels as good as possible, but it never feels perfect everywhere. There’s always a bit of give and take, and you have to get comfortable with that compromise.

“For me on Friday, the track knowledge will definitely help. Having raced there before gives me a reference for the layout and the different sections – although it’s been seven years since I was last here, so I’m sure the bumps have changed in that time!

“There are similarities and differences between driving an F1 car and an IndyCar, and some of that familiarity with the circuit will carry over. At the same time, you have to be open to what each car needs from you. I haven’t been able to compare the two cars on the same track yet, so it will be interesting to see where the approach feels similar and where you need to adapt.”

The Key Section: Turn 19

COTA provides thrills and spills at Turns 1 and 12, but the corner that really does the heavy lifting is Turn 19. The penultimate corner is a quick, open left-hander, turning through 90°, with a tendency to fling cars out wide into the run-off. Slightly downhill on entry, it’s very difficult to judge.

It comes at the end of the stadium section, when the tyres are really protesting, and anyone who’s taken a little too much out of the rubber runs the risk of running off on exit and collecting a track limits penalty.

On race day, it’s produced some spectacular attack and defence. The previous three turns are cumulatively one long right-hand bend, and often cars will approach T19 side-by-side, and have to settle their differences in braking and line for the corner – much to the delight of the large grandstand sited here.

Another facet of the corner is where it sits in relation to the all-important detection points. In years past, the DRS detection point for the main straight came just in front of the braking zone for T19. This year, the Overtake Mode detection point comes after it – so following closely through this corner is going to be important – but in a slightly different way.

The Greatest Race: 2015 US Grand Prix

The US Grand Prix has had more than its fair share of gripping title deciders and close finishes, but limiting ourselves to just the races at COTA, then the 2015 US Grand Prix really stands out, thanks to a lady named Patricia.

Patricia was a Category 5 hurricane that battered the western coast of Mexico. It was a monster, with record wind speeds and the lowest sea-level pressure recorded in the Western Hemisphere. COTA didn’t get the full force, but the City of Austin received torrential rains and flooding.

FP1 and FP3 were wet, FP2 was cancelled. Qualifying was washed-out, postponed until Sunday morning and then cancelled after Q2. Going in, Lewis Hamilton led the Drivers’ Championship with Mercedes team mate Nico Rosberg and Ferrari’s Sebastian Vettel still in mathematical contention.

Rosberg took pole, Hamilton second and Vettel, courtesy of an engine penalty, starting 13th. The race featured a wet start, the only dry running of the weekend, two Safety Car periods, two Virtual Safety Car Periods and six changes of the lead.

A start on intermediate tyres saw Hamilton grab the lead, nerfing Rosberg into the run-off at Turn 1 in the process. He was down to fifth, but the craziness of the first lap saw a VSC deployed to allow marshals to sweep up debris. With the track drying, the Red Bulls of Daniel Ricciardo and Dany Kvyat had all the pace. Danny Ric passed his team mate and then both Mercedes to take the lead on Lap 15.

Hamilton was the first of the leading pack to pit for slicks, coming in on Lap 18. Ricciardo, Rosberg and Kvyat followed the next time around, all coming out ahead of Hamilton. The advantage reversed on the slicks, however, and first Rosberg and then Hamilton were able to pass the Red Bulls and take the lead of the race.

A Lap 27 Safety Car compressed the field again, then another VSC came out on Lap 38 for more debris. Rosberg came in for a second stop. Hamilton assumed the lead, making his second stop on Lap 43 under a full Safety Car after a massive shunt for Kvyat, handing the lead back to Rosberg.

The final interruption bunched the field, effectively turning the race into a ten-lap sprint. Rosberg held his lead at the restart, but a lap later and under pressure, ran wide, allowing Hamilton to finally and decisively retake the lead, win the race, take the title, and let everyone else breathe again.

The Strategic Masterstroke

2021 US Grand Prix – Verstappen’s well-informed undercut

The stakes were high in 2021, with reigning champion Lewis Hamilton and young pretender Max Verstappen locked in battle for the Drivers’ title. Max had taken the lead of the Championship at the previous round in Turkey, and the fight resumed at COTA with Max taking pole position, with Lewis right alongside.

Hamilton made the better start and took the lead through a closely contested first corner, but the race was always going to be decided on pit stops. Degradation was expected to be high, which creates conditions for both a two-stop race and also a very powerful undercut. The risk with the undercut, however, is going too early.

There’s both the simple equation of having to extend the subsequent stints, but also the need to push the tyres straight out of the wrapper to make the undercut effective, contrary to the best use of the tyre which demands a gentle introduction for a long life. Unable to find a way through, Verstappen pitted on Lap 10 – first of the leaders to pull the pin. Hamilton waited until Lap 13 and came out six seconds behind.

Both drivers were planning a medium>hard>hard race. Lewis closed the gap but Max once again jumped early, this time pre-empting an undercut by stopping on Lap 29. Hamilton, in free air, ran to Lap 37, building a big tyre delta to ensure a good pace advantage for the final stint.

He came out nine seconds behind and again started closing the gap… but not fast enough. Verstappen had enough life left in his tyres to eke-out his lead, keeping Hamilton out of DRS range until the penultimate lap. He and Red Bull had judged the life of the hard compound perfectly.

This wasn’t down to luck. One of the inherent risks of the modern tyre allocation is that each car only gets two sets of hard compound tyres, which, at high-deg tracks, often gives teams a difficult choice to make: use a set in practice and go into the race with good information but only one set of hards, or save both for the race and effectively go in blind.

Mercedes, in common with McLaren, Ferrari, Williams, and AlphaTauri, elected save their hards for the race; Red Bull decided to learn about the tyre in practice – but only on Sergio Perez’s car. The Mexican driver was not entirely thrilled with his sacrificial role – but it enabled his team to win the Grand Prix.

title: Stunned Max Verstappen yanked from F1 cooldown room as podium revoked
excerpt:
In 2017, Max Verstappen appeared to be heading for third place in the United States after a mind-blowing pass on Kimi Räikkönen on the final lap. Nothing could have been further from the truth...

Nine years ago, the Circuit of the Americas delivered one of the most dramatic finishes of Max Verstappen's early career.

At the 2017 United States Grand Prix, the Dutchman, then just 19, appeared to have pulled off a stunning last-lap move to claim third place. The celebrations lasted only a few minutes.

Verstappen had started that race from P16 on the grid after picking up a grid penalty for exceeding his allocation of power unit components.

A sharp strategy and strong race pace helped him carve through the field, and by the closing stages he had Kimi Räikkönen in his sights in the battle for the final podium spot.

On the 56th and final lap, Verstappen pounced at Turn 17. He dived down the inside of the Finn, running all four wheels wide of the white line at the edge of the circuit.

The move handed him third place across the line, a piece of overtaking that briefly had the paddock buzzing, though it was always likely to draw scrutiny given where it had happened.

Driver

Max Verstappen

Dutch

3

Penalty strikes

The stewards, as it turned out, took a dim view of the move. They ruled that Verstappen had gained a lasting advantage over Räikkönen by leaving the track, and handed him a five-second time penalty.

The complication was timing. The penalty was only confirmed after Verstappen had already made his way to the podium area.

He had been taken to the cooldown room, the space reserved for the top three finishers ahead of the trophy presentation, when the penalty was applied to his race time. It dropped him from third to fourth in the official classification, behind Räikkönen.

What followed was an awkward scene played out in front of the cameras: Verstappen was pulled out of the cooldown room on the spot to make way for Räikkönen, who was handed his podium place moments before the ceremony got underway.

It was not the first time Verstappen had been removed from the cooldown room in such circumstances. A year earlier, at the 2016 Mexican Grand Prix, the same thing had happened, with the then-teenager demoted after the fact to fourth place behind Daniel Ricciardo following a clash with Sebastian Vettel.

Lewis Hamilton won the 2017 race from pole position, controlling much of the Grand Prix after briefly losing the lead to Vettel on the opening lap before reclaiming it and cruising to his ninth win of that season.

Vettel finished second for Ferrari, with Räikkönen ultimately classified third and Verstappen fourth. Hamilton's victory, combined with Valtteri Bottas finishing fifth, was enough to seal Mercedes' fourth consecutive constructors' championship.

title: How F1 helps Kimi Antonelli avoid breaking the law in the United States
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli stands a good chance of finishing on the podium at the United States Grand Prix this weekend, but he cannot legally drink the champagne. So what does F1 do to keep drivers under the local drinking age from breaking the law?

Kimi Antonelli could celebrate becoming Formula 1 drivers' champion at this weekend's United States Grand Prix, but the Mercedes driver will have to make do without the traditional champagne.

The 20-year-old Italian heads to the Circuit of the Americas with a 102-point championship lead over team-mate George Russell, with an opportunity to secure his maiden drivers' crown.

Even if he does not clinch the title but reaches the podium in Austin, he will have to make do with breaking from tradition.

Antonelli remains below the legal drinking age of 21 in the United States, meaning F1 must provide an alcohol-free alternative.

What will Kimi Antonelli drink on the Austin F1 podium?

Antonelli is expected to receive a non-alcoholic substitute, potentially sparkling rose water, rather than the Moët & Chandon champagne traditionally used during podium celebrations.

The precise beverage has not been confirmed, although F1 already has procedures for accommodating drivers who cannot legally consume alcohol.

The Mercedes driver encountered the same situation after winning the Miami Grand Prix in May, when he was 19.

Antonelli celebrated with an unbranded bottle containing a non-alcoholic drink, allowing him to participate in the customary podium spraying.

© XPBimages

Which F1 countries have higher legal drinking ages?

The United States has a minimum drinking age of 21, meaning Antonelli will face the same restriction at the Las Vegas Grand Prix and at Miami again in 2027, when he will still be 20.

Japan also presented a problem earlier this season, when Antonelli was 19 and below its legal drinking age of 20.

Other young drivers can face similar restrictions, including Arvid Lindblad, who is still only 19. However, the Racing Bulls driver has yet to reach the F1 rostrum.

Which F1 grands prix do not use champagne?

Alcohol is not used during podium ceremonies at the Bahrain, Saudi Arabian, Qatar and Abu Dhabi Grands Prix, where rose water is traditionally sprayed instead.

These arrangements reflect local cultural and religious considerations and apply to every driver, regardless of age.

Consequently, even established champions such as Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton must swap champagne for an alcohol-free alternative at those events.

For Antonelli, however, Austin could provide the unusual spectacle of a newly crowned world champion celebrating one of motorsport's greatest achievements without being legally old enough to drink champagne.

title: Departing F1 driver tells sport where to go with future rules
excerpt:
Outgoing F1 driver Esteban Ocon has offered a novel solution to the sport's future engine debate following the heavy criticism that has shrouded the current season.

F1's hybrid power units have faced sustained criticism this year for the severe energy derate drivers experience on straights when batteries deplete, sometimes dropping from over 1,000 horsepower to around 550 horsepower.

The current regulations split power roughly 52:48 between a 1.6-litre turbocharged V6 producing around 400 kW, and a 350 kW electric motor, after the costly MGU-H was scrapped to cut costs and attract new manufacturers such as Audi.

But the system has drawn fire from teams and drivers alike over time, notably over extreme closing-speed differences and the need for lift-and-coast energy harvesting through corners, prompting the FIA to review the deployment parameters.

Ocon, who leaves Haas at the end of this season after two years with the team but is hopeful of staying in F1 in some capacity for 2027, even if a reserve role proves necessary, has floated an unconventional alternative when discussing the engine debate.

"We're all thinking about V8s, V10s, obviously naturally aspirated," said Ocon, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365. "That's probably the best drivability you can get.

"But with Formula 1 nowadays, the amount of power we get, we might be lacking a bit of torque on the bottom end. And that's where the hybrid technology comes into play, and that's where it fills the lack of torque that this engine would have.

"So I think the best supercars in the market are the ones with a loud engine filled with a bit of electric.

"Or you don't go electric at all, and you put turbos on it, like two, one small, one big, so you feel the lag at the bottom end.

"But on a race car, I haven't seen many biturbo winning machines, so it would be quite interesting.

"Anyway, I think there are so many possibilities on the engine side and possibilities that could be better than what we have now."

[Article continues below]

Alonso urges pragmatism

Aston Martin driver Fernando Alonso, who raced in F1 during the V8 and V10 eras before the sport turned to turbo-hybrids, struck a more measured tone when asked about reverting to the old formula.

"The world has changed," the Spaniard said.

"Obviously, they were fun cars to drive, very light, very loud, but maybe they don't fit with today's world, that kind of technology.

"And we were changing engines when I started. We had an engine for Saturday, 12 laps in quali, and then an engine for Sunday. So is that possible in today's world? Probably not.

"We need to be happy and adapt to the world, and maybe the hybrid systems are the way to go.

"We just need to find the ratio of the combustion and electric parts, how much we need to help on the electric side."

title: Max Verstappen offers old-fashioned solution to 'deciding lap time' in F1
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has called for Formula 1 to strip away the layers of energy management that now shape every lap, arguing the sport has strayed too far from the basics of driving.

Four-time F1 champion Verstappen has been among the most vocal critics of the current power unit regulations, which scrapped the MGU-H and pushed the MGU-K's output to 350 kW as part of a near 50/50 split between combustion and electrical power.

The change was designed to draw new manufacturers into the sport and boost road relevance, but it has also forced drivers into heavy energy conservation, including lifting, downshifting on straights and managing battery deployment rather than simply racing flat out.

Speaking to the media, including RacingNews365, the Red Bull explained that even routine moments on track, such as pulling away at the start, have become complicated by the software running in the background.

"The start-up procedure can take four or five seconds," said Verstappen. "Then normally you can just drive off.

"The problem is there is all the software in the background that can make you not pull away, or there is a glitch, or whatever. Even on slow laps, there's stuff that can happen.

"When you cross the line, you should be able to lift off and not worry about charging your battery or making sure that it's hitting the top of the pack at the right time.

"Or at the start as well, being sure that the battery is in the right place, and in an overtake, that the battery needs to be in the right place.

"You shouldn't be thinking about where to lift off, or to go down the gear to make sure that you have better deployment."

[Article continues below]

Verstappen - 'Not what racing should be about'

Verstappen went on to argue that such calculations have no place in the sport at its purest.

"All these kinds of things, that's not what racing should be about," said Verstappen. "You should be able to go out, have a brake pedal and a throttle pedal, and that's what decides the lap time."

Verstappen's comments come after the FIA and power unit manufacturers were forced into a mid-season intervention, adjusting deployment and boost parameters after driver feedback and simulator work flagged dramatic closing speeds and cars slowing abruptly on full-throttle straights.

The FIA has since agreed phased adjustments over the next two seasons, moving to a 60-40 split in 2028, to rebalance future power units back toward the combustion engine.

For Verstappen, the appeal is straightforward: a simpler car, with lap time decided by driver input alone.

title: F1 paddock turned upside down after unexpected disqualifications — On This Day
excerpt:
Three years ago today, F1's classification sheet at Circuit of the Americas was torn up hours after the chequered flag, when Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc were both thrown out of the 2023 United States Grand Prix for running illegal plank wear.

Max Verstappen had already done the hard work on track, taking his 50th career win despite battling brake trouble, fending off Lando Norris and holding firm as Hamilton charged through to apparent second place.

But Hamilton's result lasted only as long as it took the FIA to run its post-race checks.

Scrutineers found that both the Mercedes and the Ferrari breached Article 3.5.9 e) of the Technical Regulations, which governs the thickness of the plank fitted beneath the car's floor.

The regulation permits wear down to a minimum of 9.0mm from a baseline of 10.0mm, and both cars measured below that threshold.

The selection that changed the result

The FIA had picked Hamilton's and Leclerc's cars for physical inspection based on telemetry and performance data suggesting excessive bottoming during the race, Autosport reported. Once both failed, the FIA extended checks to Verstappen's and Norris's cars to establish whether the problem ran deeper. Those two passed.

Mercedes and Ferrari did not contest the measurements. Both teams pointed to COTA's notoriously bumpy surface and the sprint weekend format, which left just a single practice session to settle ride height before parc fermé locked everything in, according to The Race.

Ferrari's head of track engineering, Diego Ioverno, admitted the margin was wafer-thin. "Our car was below the minimum threshold by a few tenths [of a millimetre], but enough to bring the stewards to consider [our car] illegal," he said.

"With hindsight, rewinding the weekend, we may have lifted even more of the car, but we would have lost performance, and we are here always to try to optimise our own performance."

Leclerc, demoted from third to a non-score, took the outcome without complaint.

"The car was not touching at all, then obviously with high fuel, etc. Then you get to the race, and you get disqualified for the smallest margin possible," he explained. "But rules are rules, and they are written in black and white, so it's completely fair to be disqualified."

Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff struck a similar tone, framing it as a lesson rather than an injustice.

"Others got it right where we got it wrong, and there's no wiggle room in the rules," he said. "We need to take it on the chin, do the learning, and come back stronger next weekend."

Hamilton, stripped of what would have been a strong recovery drive from third on the grid, called the outcome disappointing but not damning. "It is of course disappointing to be disqualified post-race, but that doesn't take away from the progress we've made this weekend," he said.

He later went further, suggesting the grid's issue was wider than two cars. "I have heard from different sources that there were many cars that had not been tested and were also illegal," Hamilton said. Nico Hülkenberg admitted he "might have been illegal myself," while Verstappen defended the wider field, pointing to the sprint format's single practice session as the root cause rather than any deliberate rule-bending.

[Article continues below]

Sargeant's solitary point

The disqualifications rippled all the way down the order. Norris was elevated to second, Carlos Sainz to third, and at the back of the points, Logan Sargeant was promoted to tenth, scoring the only point of his Formula 1 career.

"It's amazing to score my first point in F1 on home turf after the challenging weekend I've had," Sargeant said. "I'm so proud of this team and myself for the hard work and progress we've been making this season."

The American driver, dropped by Williams midway through the following season, never added to that solitary point.

The FIA's Tim Goss later explained why only two cars were checked that day rather than the whole field. "The check takes a while, and we found that they were the wrong side of the regulations. That caused us some concern," he said, adding that a full plank inspection requires partial disassembly taking roughly half an hour per car, making a grid-wide check impractical within race-day timeframes.

No regulation change followed directly from the Austin fallout, though the sprint parc fermé rules were loosened for 2024, splitting the window to give teams a setup adjustment between the sprint and qualifying, a shift widely linked in the paddock to the very trap that caught out Hamilton and Leclerc in Texas.

title: Mercedes detail latest F1 approach after unusual car experiment
excerpt:
Mercedes ran two different car specifications last time out in Singapore.

Mercedes has confirmed that it will run the upgraded specification of the W17 car in the United States this weekend.

The Brackley-based squad was defeated at the last two rounds in Malaysia and Singapore, with Red Bull and Max Verstappen taking back-to-back wins.

Wolff sends Mercedes warning as double title success looms

Although the Silver Arrows have won the US Grand Prix five times since the start of the hybrid era, the team's last victory at the Circuit of the Americas came in 2019.

As Mercedes seeks to close out a strong season on a high note, Wolff insisted it can't afford to relax its approach.

"The United States Grand Prix begins another demanding triple-header," he said.

"There is plenty at stake, but we won't get ahead of ourselves.

"The priority is the weekend in front of us: execute well, maximise our performance and take each race as it comes."

title: Helmut Marko lashes out at Christian Horner: 'An embarrassment'
excerpt:
Helmut Marko has hit out at Christian Horner for releasing his autobiography 'Drive' on the anniversary of Red Bull founder Dietrich Mateschitz's death.

Helmut Marko has accused Christian Horner of poor taste for releasing his autobiography Drive on 22 October, the fourth anniversary of Dietrich Mateschitz's death.

The former Red Bull advisor branded the timing "an embarrassment" and dismissed the book's contents as a "low-calibre" collection of untruths, though he declined to engage with its specific allegations.

Horner's memoir, published today, has reopened one of Formula 1's bitterest internal feuds.

In it, the former Red Bull principal accuses Marko of leaking sensitive intellectual and operational details to the press, claiming Adrian Newey grew so frustrated by the disclosures that senior staff began withholding information from Marko in meetings.

Horner also recounts the moment of his own dismissal in 2025, alleging Marko stood alongside Oliver Mintzlaff and repeated the corporate line "it's about the can" when explaining the decision.

'Low-calibre' claims

Speaking to Krone, Marko refused to pick through the book point by point: "That's a collection of untruths of such a low calibre that I won't address them."

He did, however, want to correct one specific claim.

"I only want to correct one claim: that I did indeed offer my condolences after the death of his ex-partner Beverly," he said whilst — according to Krone — showing the corresponding message on his phone.

Horner had written in Drive that Marko never reached out after Beverly's passing last year, during what he described as an already painful period, as Marko worked to have him removed from Red Bull. Horner called the lack of contact "not very classy" at the time.

The rift between the pair traces back to the power struggle that followed Mateschitz's death in October 2022, which split the team between Horner's camp, backed by majority shareholder Chalerm Yoovidhya, and Marko's Austrian faction.

Horner has since described all contact with Marko as having gone silent since his final day at the factory, insisting their parting handshake was the last word exchanged between them.

Marko added: "And the fact that the book is being published on the very day Dietrich Mateschitz died is an embarrassment."

title: Red Bull handed 'pretty cool' verdict after striking first-year success

Red Bull Powertrains has earned recognition it "deserves" after recent victories for Max Verstappen in Bahrain and Singapore.

title: FIA president puts fresh timeline on V8 return decision for F1
excerpt:
FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has outlined that he hopes the framework for a V8 return in the early 2030s will be confirmed in the coming months.

Several drivers have criticised the 2026 power units since their introduction, with complaints centring on heavy battery dependence and energy-management demands.

Max Verstappen has been among the most vocal, alongside Fernando Alonso, Lewis Hamilton and Lando Norris, who have all questioned the current regulations.

The complaints have fed into wider discussions about overhauling the engine formula beyond the current cycle, with the sport now touted to return to V8 engines as part of the next set of regulations.

Asked whether a new regulatory framework would be agreed this year, Ben Sulayem told media including RacingNews365: "Yes, yes. In a few months, hopefully."

"Of course, you push the teams and the PUMs to come back to you, and we will wait for them to come back to us."

Ben Sulayem made striking comments in Rwanda last week, where he declared that V8s would return for 2030.

But the FIA president has since updated his comments, making it clear that nothing has been formally agreed yet, stressing that several technical and financial factors still need resolving before any switch to simpler V8 engines is confirmed.

"No, not yet, but it will be,” he added.

"The consultation has been a lot. The papers are with the teams. Teams are reading it. Team principals, PUMs, power unit manufacturers. A driver has been consulted about it."

"When you make it simpler, and then you make it half the price, the R&D doesn't just go down by half, but then the simplicity that comes with it, the production can take shorter time."

"So, there are materials also... the down of an engine, which is a block, it's only for reliability. You go up, and then it's the power."

"That's where you have to limit things, because limitation of the power means you have to police so that nobody can use certain materials."

"Certain materials can be very expensive if you're trying to get those last few horsepower. The sound will be there and then a very light car, but you have to be very careful of how light you can let it."

title: 'Drive' - a review of Christian Horner's long-awaited F1 memoir
excerpt:
RacingNews365 has read Christian Horner's new F1 memoir - Drive. This is what we made of it.

22 October 8:20AM

If you are expecting Christian Horner's new F1 memoir Drive to be a drive-by shooting of those who decided to remove him from Red Bull, a settling of old scores, and a load of soapy waffle, painting himself as the martyr who was stunned as the sword was twisted in, then this is not the book for you.

Given Horner's 20-year stint at the helm of one of F1's most successful teams and his status as one of the most successful team principals in history, his first book was always going to be an intriguing read.

Throw in the manner of his sudden departure from Red Bull after being sacked in 2025, and all the ingredients are there for an unrivalled look at the politics which have dominated F1 over the last two decades, by a man usually responsible for lobbing a hand grenade or two into topics of the day.

Again, those expecting Horner to air all the dirty linen of his Red Bull sacking are going to be mistaken. Yes, it is covered towards the end of the book, as is his initial reaction to allegations of improper behaviour levied against him in early 2024 - and which he has always strenuously denied, with investigations from leading KCs also not upholding the complaint - but it is not the central pillar of the book.

Rather, it is how the wannabe F1 driver, who once bumped into Nigel Mansell and Ayrton Senna after sneaking into a Silverstone test, turned what Lewis Hamilton branded a "fizzy energy drink" team into one of the greatest grand prix teams of all time.

Perhaps the most striking moment for your writer was something Horner mentions very early on after being handed the keys to Red Bull Racing by Dietrich Mateschitz in 2005.

He tells of waiting in the car park at Milton Keynes and watching Tony Purnell and David Pitchforth leave for the last time, having been dismissed by Jaguar.

Fast forward 20-and-a-half-years, "not bad for a number two driver", Brazil 2012 and the lead-up to Multi-21, the horror of Renault's turbo hybrids, Abu Dhabi 2021, and the breach of the cost cap later, Horner describes sitting in his office for the final time, and seeing Helmut Marko and Oliver Mintzlaff waiting for him to "presumably exit the same way Tony and David" had.

It is a full-circle moment as Horner invites Marko in, with the veteran Austrian then "parroting" the company line of "it's about the can" when asked why the decision had been taken now.

[Review continues below]

© XPBimages

Christian Horner book review

Perhaps of all the figures in the book, it is Marko for whom you get the sense the knives were sharpened, but Horner doesn't go for the full all-out attack.

Sure, there are interesting tidbits, like how, in the early days of Adrian Newey joining, he expressed his disdain for how so much intellectual Red Bull information was leaked to the press by Marko, who treated information "as currency." This led to Horner claiming senior Red Bull figures were then "selective" about the information shared in meetings with Marko.

Horner expresses his doubt about Marko's driver decisions, especially saying he was "uncomfortable" with the choice to promote Liam Lawson in 2025, and provided insight into the racism row which erupted when Marko claimed Sergio Perez, from Mexico, in North America, did not have the same mindset as Europeans Sebastian Vettel and Max Verstappen "because he is South American."

Another character who you perhaps get the sense that there is plenty more to say about is Jos Verstappen, but Horner keeps his powder dry, with no love lost between the two.

There are major revelations like how Horner wanted to sign Fernando Alonso, Charles Leclerc, and Carlos Sainz, only to be rebuffed at all times, and how in 2012, Niki Lauda offered him the job of Mercedes team principal - something Horner rejected and instead went to his great sparring partner, Toto Wolff.

The book does not skip over the key events of Horner's latter reign, including the decision to scrap the potential tie-up with Porsche - over which Marko threatened to sack Horner if he voiced his displeasure to the Thai majority owner, Chalerm Yoovidhya - and how Red Bull Powertrains was formed.

Overall, Drive is a solid retrospective on the F1 career of a figure who has been one of the most influential figures in grand prix history.

The paddock is a sorer place without Horner, a man who knew how to press all the right buttons of his rivals, having been to the school of Bernie Ecclestone, Max Mosley, Ron Dennis, and Jean Todt.

He recalls some of that in Drive, and it makes the book a great read for F1 fans, young or old. Just don't expect a copy to be heading to the Graz home of one H. Marko...

Drive by Christian Horner is published on October 22nd by Penguin.

title: Why F1 delaying Middle East decision could avoid awkward title scenario
excerpt:
Formula 1 still needs to make a definitive call on whether to head to the Middle East to end the season or pivot to Imola instead. However, the timing of that decision could have championship-defining ramifications.

22 October 7:25AM

Formula 1's delay in deciding the fate of the Qatar and Abu Dhabi Grands Prix could help the championship avoid an awkward scenario in which Kimi Antonelli is crowned F1 drivers' champion away from a race weekend.

With the Mercedes driver closing in on the 2026 title, the timing of any decision to cancel the final two rounds of the season and replace them with a standalone event at Imola could have significant implications.

If F1 opts to invoke its contingency plan before the Mexico City Grand Prix on November 1, Antonelli could be declared champion without turning a wheel that weekend.

Depending on how the next two rounds unfold, the Italian could even have already secured the title at the United States Grand Prix in Austin, with the decision to reduce the number of remaining races merely confirming his achievement.

Waiting until the build-up to the São Paulo Grand Prix would significantly reduce the likelihood of such a scenario, allowing the title battle to play out on track before any announcement is made.

However, the situation is not entirely straightforward, and F1 must balance the sporting implications against the practicalities of making a late calendar change.

The championship has so far signalled its intention to complete its 2026 campaign as planned, with the Qatar and Abu Dhabi Grands Prix forming the final two legs of the year-ending triple-header, which begins in Las Vegas.

Nevertheless, ongoing instability in the Middle East means F1 cannot rule out a late cancellation. Safety remains the overriding consideration, and if the assurances provided by the Gulf states are deemed insufficient, F1 could turn to Imola as an alternative venue to conclude the season.

Time is becoming an increasingly important factor. Although the teams would not rely on sea freight for the proposed alternative, with air freight required, the wider logistical operation would still need sufficient time to be organised.

Planning for both eventualities is already under way, but the anticipated mid-October deadline for a definitive decision has passed. F1 is therefore running short of time to settle the matter.

[Article continues below]

Why the timing of F1's decision matters for Antonelli

Antonelli currently holds a 102-point advantage in the drivers’ championship and is on the brink of becoming the sport’s youngest world champion.

The mathematics are relatively straightforward under the existing calendar. If he leaves the Circuit of the Americas with a lead of at least 125 points over his nearest rival, whether that is team-mate George Russell, Lewis Hamilton or Max Verstappen, the title will be his.

That is a sizeable margin to make up in a single weekend, making the following round in Mexico City the more likely venue for Antonelli to secure the championship.

If he leaves the Mexico City Grand Prix with a lead of at least 100 points, the title fight will be over, with four rounds remaining on the original schedule.

But the calculations change if Qatar and Abu Dhabi are cancelled and replaced by a single race weekend at Imola.

With only five rounds remaining after Austin under the revised schedule, Antonelli would need a lead of 100 points to become champion immediately after the United States Grand Prix. In other words, if he leaves Austin with a lead of more than 99 points, a decision to reduce the calendar before the Mexico City Grand Prix would mathematically crown him champion before the next race.

That is the awkward situation F1 could avoid by holding off on its announcement.

If the championship waits until the build-up to the São Paulo Grand Prix, Antonelli would have another opportunity to secure the title on track in Mexico. Even if the Italian had already accumulated enough points to clinch the championship in Austin, the formal decision to reduce the remaining schedule would come after the Mexico City Grand Prix weekend.

The delay would not change when Antonelli had mathematically secured the title, but it could avoid the optics of a championship being decided by an administrative announcement rather than the outcome of a race weekend.

[Article continues below]

© XPB Images

The remaining risk in F1's title scenario

There is, however, no guarantee that delaying the decision until Brazil would resolve the problem.

The situation becomes more complicated if Antonelli has a difficult couple of weekends in Austin and Mexico City, allowing his advantage to shrink.

If his lead falls to between 75 and 99 points after the Mexico City Grand Prix, a decision to replace Qatar and Abu Dhabi with Imola before the São Paulo Grand Prix could still mathematically crown him champion before any track action at Interlagos.

A further loss of ground in Brazil would create similar complications if F1 had still not confirmed its plans.

Ultimately, the championship must make its calendar decision based on safety, logistics and the assurances it receives about holding the final two rounds in the Middle East. The drivers’ championship cannot dictate that decision.

Nevertheless, the timing of the announcement matters. Waiting until after Mexico would give Antonelli a greater opportunity to settle the title on track, while allowing F1 to avoid an unnecessarily awkward conclusion to a season in which the championship could be decided by a calendar change rather than a chequered flag.

title: Max Verstappen handed Red Bull boost with 'no weakness' verdict
excerpt:
Red Bull has been enjoying a hot streak of form of late, which it will be hoping to carry over to Austin this weekend.

Former F1 driver Jolyon Palmer has labelled Max Verstappen as the favourite heading into the United States Grand Prix this weekend.

Verstappen enters the event having won the previous two rounds in Malaysia and Singapore, Red Bull's only victories this year.

The team struggled for form throughout much of the campaign, however recent upgrades have allowed it to get itself back in the mix at the head of the order.

When asked if Verstappen should be considered the favourite for the US Grand Prix, Palmer told the F1 Nation podcast: "I think so.

"The fact that they can be so good in the low speed... Singapore is bumpy.

"You also need to ride the kerbs pretty heavily, that's been a weakness of Red Bull. The low-speed cornering we saw in Baku was pretty good.

"Straight-line speed generally seems to be pretty strong, which we saw in Baku and Malaysia. In Malaysia, we saw the high-speed cornering wasn't bad.

"Ferrari were king of the corners in Singapore and Malaysia when you compare their laps to Max, but the overall package that Ferrari has means that the power unit is still such a hindrance."

[Article continues below]

Throughout the year, it was regular to hear Verstappen voice his complaints over the team radio.

But Palmer highlighted that his concerns have calmed of late, labelling it as a key indicator that the car has improved.

With the team introducing its final major upgrade of the year in Baku, Palmer suggested it now seems free of weakness.

"I look at the Red Bull with the upgrades and the weaknesses that we used to hear don't seem to be there.

"They're good at kerb riding. I think Max mentioned once [about] the downshifts in Singapore, but they've been able to dial that out for years anyway.

"The other thing is, I wondered if Singapore might expose their ability to set the car up on a Friday because often we've seen for the last couple of years they're a little bit head-scratching on Friday, turn it around for a Saturday.

"But they were good from the first moment. No guarantee that will carry over, but right now, I don't see a weakness in it."

title: Ferrari unveil fresh F1 livery in special one-off 'blueprint' design
excerpt:
Ferrari has become the latest team to unveil a special livery for the United States Grand Prix this weekend.

The new colour scheme "celebrates the creative and engineering process that transforms an idea into a Formula 1 car," and designed in conjuction with Ferrari's title sponsor, HP.

The design "draws inspiration from the belief that every Ferrari begins with a line on paper," read a team statement, with sketches, technical drawings and blueprint-inspired graphics that are normally hidden beneath the finished bodywork, offering a visual tribute to the designers, engineers and technicians whose work lies behind every performance achievement."

It is not its first one-off livery used by Ferrari this year, having also created a new concept for its home race in Italy last month.

Ferrari has joined fellow front-runners Mercedes, as well as the two American teams Haas and Cadillac, in launching a fresh design for the event around the Circuit of the Americas.

The Italian squad enters the weekend hoping to fight for its third race victory of the campaign, having last stood on the top step of the podium at Silverstone.

Lewis Hamilton is the most successful driver around COTA, winning the grand prix five times - although his last win at the venue came in 2017.

Team-mate Charles Leclerc is also a winner around the track, triumphing at the 2024 edition of the race.
